What makes a pine tree so fascinating?

Green even in winter, the pine tree is one of the most familiar trees to us. Amazing science is packed into its needle-like leaves and its pinecones.

content.alt: Pine Tree - Nature and science facts about pine trees
content.text:
Nature and science facts about pine trees

Pine needles are thin like needles and covered in a thick coating, so they photosynthesize even in winter. Pinecone scales open and close with humidity — they open wide when it's dry to release seeds, and close when it rains to protect them. The resin in the trunk has antibacterial properties that seal wounds, and when it hardens underground it becomes the gem amber. The roots live in partnership with pine mushroom fungi.

Parent guide — extending into observation and hands-on play

Pick up a pinecone, soak it in water and then let it dry, and watch the scales close and open for yourself (a truly amazing experiment!). Feel the texture of the needles and smell the resin, too.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why does a pinecone open and close?
A. Because it responds to humidity. It opens when it's dry to release seeds, and closes when it rains to protect them.

Q. Why is a pine tree green even in winter?
A. Because its needle leaves are covered in a thick coating, so they can keep photosynthesizing even in the cold winter.

Q. How can we observe it at home?
A. Soak a pinecone in water and let it dry to watch it close and open, and feel the texture of the needles and the smell of the resin.
